concepts.title: The Versatile Nature of Carbon - Covalent Bonding
concepts.definition: Carbon forms millions of compounds because it bonds covalently by sharing electrons, needs four electrons to complete its octet (tetravalency), and links with other carbons in chains and rings (catenation) - giving single, double and triple bonded structures in enormous variety.
concepts.key_idea: Share, not transfer: tetravalent carbon catenates into the endless chemistry of life.
concepts.textbook_ref: jesc104.txt sections on covalent bonding and the versatile nature of carbon

solution_steps.explain: Carbon holds four, so it shares four more to complete the octet.
Electron dot structures show the shared pairs as bonds.
Carbon-carbon bonds build chains, branches and rings.

concepts.title: Hydrocarbons, Functional Groups and Homologous Series
concepts.definition: Compounds of carbon and hydrogen are hydrocarbons - saturated alkanes with single bonds and unsaturated alkenes and alkynes with multiple bonds; attaching functional groups like alcohol, aldehyde, ketone or carboxylic acid creates families called homologous series, where successive members differ by CH2.
concepts.key_idea: Same functional group, CH2 steps: a homologous series is carbon's family album.
concepts.textbook_ref: jesc104.txt sections on hydrocarbons, functional groups, homologous series

solution_steps.explain: Single bonds mean alkane; double or triple mean alkene or alkyne.
OH, CHO, CO or COOH groups name the family.
Add CH2 to move to the next homologue.

concepts.title: Chemical Properties and Reactions of Carbon Compounds
concepts.definition: Carbon compounds burn in oxygen releasing heat and light, oxidise to alcohols and acids, add hydrogen in the presence of catalysts, and combine with acids in esterification - while substitution replaces hydrogen in saturated hydrocarbons like methane with chlorine.
concepts.key_idea: Combustion, oxidation, addition, substitution and esterification - the five moves of carbon chemistry.
concepts.textbook_ref: jesc104.txt section 4.3 (chemical properties of carbon compounds), ethanol and ethanoic acid

solution_steps.explain: Burning, adding, replacing or combining - classify first.
Catalysts like nickel for addition, acid for esterification.
Carbon dioxide and water for combustion; ester and water for esterification.

concepts.title: Soaps and Detergents - Cleansing Action
concepts.definition: Soap molecules have two ends - a hydrophilic head that loves water and a hydrophobic tail that loves oil; tails trap oil into micelles which water rinses away. Hard water, however, forms scum with soap, so detergents with different heads work even in hard water.
concepts.key_idea: Two-ended molecules: tail hugs oil, head hugs water - dirt leaves in micelles.
question_patterns: how does a soap molecule remove dirt - explain the micelle formation
what are the two ends of a soap molecule and what does each like
why does soap not work in hard water - explain scum formation
how do detergents differ from soaps - give the advantage
draw the structure of a soap molecule labelling its parts
what is a micelle - explain its formation during washing

solution_steps.explain: Tails push into the oil droplet, heads face the water.
Agitation wraps the oil inside a sphere of soap molecules.
Water carries the micelles off, leaving the cloth clean.
